articles.title: Crows, Moths, and Makefiles: How 300 Megabytes of Crow DNA Explains Why a 20-Kilobyte Scar File Outsmarts a Terabyte LLM
articles.description: Why do New Caledonian crows bend wire into hooks with zero training while a trillion-parameter LLM flies straight into the same production bug zapper? How Anthony Zador's Genomic Bottleneck explains what 'instinct' really is in AI coding agents.
articles.body_html:
Why can a New Caledonian crow bend a piece of wire into a hook on the first try—when no crow ancestor ever saw wire in nature—while a trillion-parameter LLM flies straight into the same 3 AM production bug zapper? Because evolution gave the crow a 20-kilobyte Makefile, and we gave the LLM a moth's porch light.

"Animals are born with highly structured brain connectivity, which enables them to learn very rapidly. Because the genome's capacity is orders of magnitude smaller than the number of synapses, the genome cannot specify the exact wiring diagram directly; instead, it specifies rules through a 'Genomic Bottleneck.'" — Anthony M. Zador, Nature Communications (2019)

"In the context of Scars, is there an equivalent of 'instinct' for an LLM? Would that be perhaps immutable parts of the training? Core knowledge? I was thinking about how crows seem to have amazing emergent problem-solving abilities, and how that must be instinct then, but how was that stored in the DNA?" — Randal L. Schwartz

1. The Betty the Crow Mystery: How Do You Store Wire-Bending in DNA?

If you have never watched the classic Oxford University footage of Betty, a New Caledonian crow (Corvus moneduloides), stop and picture the experiment (Weir, Chappell, & Kacelnik, 2002).

A small bucket of food is sitting at the bottom of a vertical glass tube. Next to the tube is a straight piece of laboratory garden wire—a human-manufactured metal alloy that zero generations of crows have ever encountered in 30 million years of evolution.

Betty picks up the straight wire, pokes it into the tube, realizes a straight shaft cannot lift the bucket handle, wedges the tip of the wire into a crevice in the tray base, pulls laterally with her beak to bend a 90-degree hook, and fishes the bucket out of the tube.

In another famous experiment (Jelbert et al., 2014), New Caledonian crows are presented with a narrow tube partially filled with water and a floating worm just out of reach—literally Aesop's Fable (The Crow and the Pitcher). Without training, the crows ignore floating Styrofoam blocks, select heavy sinking stones, and drop them one by one into the water until the displaced water level rises high enough to grab the worm.

Now ask the computer scientist's question:

How on Earth is that stored in the crow's DNA?!

Do the information-theory math—what neuroscientist Anthony Zador at Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory famously called The Genomic Bottleneck (2019):

  • A New Caledonian crow's entire genome has roughly 1.2 billion base pairs (~300 MB of raw 2-bit data—less than a single CD-ROM, and only a tiny regulatory fraction of that 300 MB specifies brain wiring).
  • Yet the crow's brain (its avian pallium) contains over a billion neurons and trillions of synaptic weights.
  • Even more baffling: you cannot store "how to bend 20th-century steel garden wire" in DNA via Darwinian selection, because no ancestral crow ever touched steel wire!

So when we say the crow solved the puzzle by "instinct," what was actually in the DNA?

And more importantly for those of us building autonomous software engineering systems: what is the equivalent of "instinct" inside an LLM? Is it the frozen pre-trained weights? The core knowledge? Or have we been confusing two completely opposite biological instincts all along?

2. Two Kinds of Biological Instinct: The Moth vs. The Crow

When software engineers talk about an LLM's "instincts," they usually point to the immutable pre-trained weights (theta)—the hundreds of gigabytes of floating-point parameters frozen during pre-training and RLHF.

After all, when you type a prompt and the LLM immediately starts emitting Python or Dart code without consulting a manual, that looks like an instinct, right?

Yes—it is the exact instinct of a moth flying into a bug zapper.

In evolutionary biology, "instinct" is not one thing. Nature evolved two fundamentally different kinds of instinct, and comparing them reveals why unscarred LLMs fail in production:

flowchart TD
    subgraph Moth["🦋 Strategy A: The Moth's Instinct (Unscarred LLM Weights)"]
        M1["Hardwired Prior in Weights:\n'Keep brightest light at constant angle α'\n(In pre-training: 'Emit highest-frequency web tutorial')"]
        M2["In Ancestral Environment (The Moon at ∞):\nFlies in a straight line (Passes 10-line LeetCode demo)"]
        M3["In Production Environment (Porch Light at 2 meters):\nLogarithmic spiral straight into the bug zapper!\n(Vector 2: The Seductive 5-6-7-8 Trap)"]
        M1 --> M2 --> M3
    end

    subgraph Crow["🐦‍⬛ Strategy B: The Crow's Instinct (Synthetic Scars + Makefile DAG)"]
        C1["1. Innate Probing Loop in DNA (~20 KB WORKFLOW.mk):\n'Pick up stick → Poke crevice → Test physical leverage'\n(Target 15 Digraph → Target 30 TDD Red → Target 35 Green)"]
        C2["2. Spinal Nociception (Tier-1 Weights + 15ms AST Sensor):\n'If branch cracks or wire slips, recoil immediately'\n(15ms Linter + Target 40 Clean-Room Critic)"]
        C3["3. Flock Cultural Scolding (SCAR_REGISTRY.md):\n'One crow sees a trap → Whole flock learns in 12 seconds'\n(Target 90 4-Vector Scar Compilation)"]
        C1 --> C2 --> C3
    end

1. The Moth's Instinct: Hardwired Phototaxis (Vector 2: The Seductive 5-6-7-8)

Why do moths fly into flames and porch lights? Moths are not suicidal. For 100 million years before humans invented candles and LED bulbs, the only bright optical source at night was the Moon at optical infinity (d -> infinity).

If a flying insect wants to travel in a straight line at night, evolution can wire a dead-simple sensorimotor rule into its ganglia:

"Keep the brightest light source at a constant 30-degree angle to your compound eye."

When the light source is 384,400 kilometers away, keeping it at a constant 30-degree angle guarantees a perfectly straight flight path.

Now put that exact same moth in a backyard with a porch light two meters away (d << infinity). If you maintain a constant 30-degree angle to a point source at finite distance, basic geometry dictates that your flight path is a logarithmic spiral (r = a × e^(b × theta)) that terminates directly inside the flame.

An unscarred LLM's pre-trained weights (theta) are statistical phototaxis:

  • During pre-training on 10 trillion web tokens, the "Moon at infinity" is the Sunny-Day Tutorial Average (Page 1 of Google / Stack Overflow). In a 20-line stateless blog post, skipping StreamSubscription.cancel(), using wall-clock DateTime.now(), or firing unguarded parallel writes works fine.
  • When you drop that LLM into a stateful, concurrent production monorepo (the porch light at two meters), its immutable weight-instinct (argmax P(token | context)) follows the exact same constant-angle tutorial prior—and spirals straight into the 3 AM bug zapper!
  • In our 4-Vector Scar taxonomy, we call this Vector 2: The Trap (The Seductive 5-6-7-8). It feels like "core knowledge" to the model, just as the porch light looks like the Moon to the moth.

2. The Crow's Instinct: How 300 MB of DNA Bootstraps Emergent Genius

Now return to our New Caledonian crow. Why didn't Betty the Crow spiral into a loop when the straight wire failed to lift the bucket?

In 2005, Oxford biologists (Kenward et al., 2005) raised juvenile New Caledonian crows in controlled isolation where they never saw an adult crow use a tool. What happened? At a specific developmental week, every single young crow spontaneously began picking up twigs, poking them into holes, and prying against surfaces!

Wait—if DNA cannot store a lookup table of wire hooks, what did the crow's genome store?

Through Zador's Genomic Bottleneck, evolution compressed three tiny, universal primitives into the crow's DNA:

  1. An Innate Epistemic Probing Loop (The Scientific Method in Motor Circuits): The genome does not encode answers; it encodes an active probing sequence: > Grab object → Poke into boundary → Apply small test force → Observe physical resistance / displacement → Adjust geometry.
  2. Endogenous Nociception & Leverage Gradients (Pain + Sub-Goal Dopamine): The crow's brain is wired so that physical slippage or pain triggers an immediate motor halt (Circuit Breaker), while seeing the target move even 2 millimeters closer fires a striatal dopamine pulse.
  3. Rapid Amygdala Tagging & Cultural Flock Transmission (Cornell, Marzluff, & Pecoraro, 2011): In wildlife biologist John Marzluff's famous University of Washington experiments, researchers wore a specific caveman mask while trapping and banding just seven crows on campus, then released them unharmed.
    • Those crows immediately encoded a permanent somatic marker for that face.
    • Better yet: when a person walked across campus wearing that mask years later, huge mobs of crows—including young crows born years after the original trapping who had never been captured themselves—recognized the mask and dive-bombed the researcher with harsh scolding calls!
    • One crow touched the stove; the entire flock inherited the scar across generations.

3. The Biological-Mechanical Rosetta Stone: Mapping the Crow to Synthetic Scars

Look closely at the three pieces of the crow's intelligence, and you will see the exact architecture of Synthetic Scars (syntheticscars.org):

Biological Component in the Crow Information Size What Role It Plays Exact Equivalent in the Synthetic Scar Architecture
0. The Single Pyramidal Neuron (DNA's Cellular ALU) 1 Cell Blueprint (Replicated 10^9×) Dendritic dot product (w · x) + GABAergic divisive normalization (`
1. The Pallial Motor & Visual Cortex Billions of Synapses ({% raw %}Terabytes) Stores massive vocabulary of objects, shapes, and candidate muscle movements—but cannot tell a safe branch from a trap on its own. The LLM's Core Pre-Trained Weights (theta): Massive cosine-similarity engine (~1 TB) holding every programming language, SDK API, and design pattern—the motor cortex, NOT the survival instinct.
2. The Genomic Bottleneck (Innate Probing Loop) Tiny Regulatory DNA (Kilobytes) Hardwires the epistemic probing instinct: "Never leap blindly; poke the crevice with a stick first and feel how reality pushes back." WORKFLOW.mk / SKILL.md (~20 KB Declarative DAG): The immutable scientific-method loop—Target 15 (poke the strict digraph blast radius) → Target 30 (write a failing tdd-red test stick) → Target 35 (make it green).
3. Spinal Nociception & Pain Reflex Brainstem / Striatal Loop Instant recoil when a branch cracks or a tool slips (-∞ barrier). Tier-1 Scar-Aligned Weights (Rapid-Regret DPO) + 15ms AST Sensors + Target 40 Clean-Room Critic.
4. Flock Cultural Scolding Calls (Marzluff's Mask) Sparse Acoustic / Amygdala Signatures One crow gets trapped once; the warning signature spreads to every crow in the territory in seconds and persists for generations. SCAR_REGISTRY.md (The 4-Vector Scars): One agent collides at Target 90; within 12 seconds, the 4-Vector Scar (Wound, Trap, Circuit Breaker, Reflex) is committed to Git so no future agent ever touches that burner again (0.0% repeat regression rate across 256 tickets).

Wait—Even the Single Biological Neuron Is a DNA-Baked Cosine-Similarity Engine!

Stop and look at Row 0 of that table, because this is where the biological-mechanical overlap becomes almost spooky.

Earlier in this series (Part 4.1), I noted that all I really want a Google TPU to do is compute cosine similarity ("finding its cosine buddies") between the riverbanks of my Makefile.

Then I stopped and asked myself: Wait... how does DNA wire a biological neuron in the first place?!

Look at the biophysics of a single pyramidal neuron in a crow's pallium or your neocortex:

  1. Dendritic Dot Products + Divisive Normalization = Biological Cosine Similarity: A neuron has thousands of incoming dendritic synapses with weights w = [w_1, ..., w_n] receiving incoming spike firing rates x = [x_1, ..., x_n]. The cell body sums the weighted inputs (w · x), while local inhibitory interneurons (GABAergic basket cells; Carandini & Heeger, 2012) divide that signal by the total population activity ||x|| (divisive normalization—nature's exact LayerNorm + softmax!) and homeostatic synaptic scaling normalizes ||w||: 
   V_membrane  ~  (w · x) / (||w|| × ||x||)  =  cos(theta)

When the angle theta between the input vector x and the synaptic weight vector w approaches 0° (cos(theta) -> 1), the soma crosses -55 mV and fires an action potential!

  1. Embryonic Wiring via Molecular Q · K^T Barcodes (Sperry, 1963): How do growing axons find the right dendrites in the embryo before the crow even hatches? Under Roger Sperry's Nobel Prize–winning Chemoaffinity Hypothesis, DNA expresses combinatorial gradients of surface receptor proteins (ephrins, cadherins, protocadherins) on the growing axon tip (Query vector Q) and the target dendrite (Key vector K). When they touch, biochemical binding affinity is literally a molecular dot product (Q · K^T)!

Evolution didn't build a symbolic logic gate in DNA. DNA baked a self-normalizing cosine-similarity unit (the neuron), stamped out a billion copies of it to form a cortex, and then used a tiny 20-kilobyte Genomic Bottleneck script (WORKFLOW.mk) to wire those cosine engines into a stick-poking, pain-avoiding survival loop.

4. Why This Answers the "1,000-Scar Scaling" Question

Whenever engineers first see our Makefile workflow (WORKFLOW.mk) and our 618-scar registry, they often ask the exact same question biologists used to ask about crows:

"Wait a minute, Randal! An LLM has a terabyte of weights, and a production codebase has millions of possible bugs. How can a 20-kilobyte Makefile workflow and 5 phase-bound scars per step possibly keep a terabyte model from breaking things?!"

Now you know the answer—Zador's Genomic Bottleneck:

Biology's Genomic Bottleneck:
  |Crow Regulatory DNA| (~KBs)
  << |Brain Synapses| (~TBs)

The Synthetic Scar Bottleneck:
  |WORKFLOW.mk + Active Scars| (~20 KB)
  << |LLM Weights| (~1 TB)

If you try to make an AI agent safe by pre-writing a massive encyclopedic rulebook of every positive answer it should ever emit, you are trying to stuff a billion synapses of lookup tables into DNA. You will blow out your 200k context window, trigger context compaction, and fail.

That is not how DNA works, and it is not how Synthetic Scars works:

  1. Let the Terabyte Weights Be the Motor Cortex: We don't need WORKFLOW.mk to teach Gemini or Claude how to write a Dart switch expression or a PostgreSQL join. That core knowledge is already sitting in the terabyte weights (theta).
  2. Use the 20-Kilobyte Makefile as the Crow's Stick-Poking Instinct: Instead of letting the LLM trust its moth-like first impulse (1-2-3-4 -> 5-6-7-8), the Makefile DAG forces the model to poke reality with a stick first:
    • "Before you touch the code, draw the strict digraph of every caller and state transition (Target 15)."
    • "Before you write the fix, prove you understand the bug by writing a test that fails (Target 30: tdd-red)."
    • "Before you ask the human to review, hand the git tree to 'Sam at the end of the hall' (Target 40: Clean-Room Adversarial Critic)."
  3. Use 4-Vector Scars as the Flock's Warning Calls: And when a specific subsystem has a hidden trap waiting in the grass (a caveman mask on campus!), SCAR_REGISTRY.md fires at the exact moment the agent reaches for the twig:
    • The Trap: "Your tutorial weights want to emit THAT..."
    • The Circuit Breaker: "STOP! You are excused from your promise to take that shortcut."

    * The Permanent Reflex: "Climb E-F-G-H (THE OTHER) instead."

Summary: Stop Waiting for a Bigger Moth

Right now, the AI industry is spending hundreds of billions of dollars trying to breed a 10-trillion-parameter moth—convinced that if the prisoner reads twice as many books inside the cell, it will finally stop flying into the porch light.

It won't. A bigger moth with sharper eyes just computes the logarithmic spiral into the bug zapper with higher mathematical precision.

Your frontier LLM already has all the raw motor cortex and syntactic knowledge in the universe. What gives it wisdom is pairing that trillion-parameter motor cortex with the compact Genomic Bottleneck of someone who has actually lived outside in the weather:

  1. An innate probing loop (WORKFLOW.mk) that pokes reality with a stick before trusting a hypothesis;
  2. Spinal nociception (SCAR-TDD-01) that recoils from false finishes; and
  3. A shared cultural flock memory (SCAR_REGISTRY.md) where the 3 AM pain of one agent becomes the permanent survival instinct of every agent that follows.

In Part 4.4, we'll look upstream at the cognitive physics behind this: why senior engineering craft lives in Be -> Do -> Have (Context -> Process -> Content), how veteran hackers use the "Null-State" couch flash and ladder rungs to avoid debugging ruts, and why guiding an AI coding agent is identical to stand-up comedy.

articles.title: Don't Write Markdown Files for Your Coding Agent. Write Scripts.
articles.description: If you want agents to do what you want, you need to learn how to box them into deterministic actions....
articles.body_html:
If you want agents to do what you want, you need to learn how to box them into deterministic actions. Unfortunately, this is not what current coding agents are good at. They are designed to be exploratory and open ended. They take a vague prompt, produce a plausible patch, run tests, loop a few times, and so on. This is great for prototyping and greenfield work. But when you need something reliable, when you want the same command to have the same effect every time, the same refactoring to happen to twenty files, the same deploy process to execute in the same order, the vague prompt and the "please read the docs" prompt become a liability.

So you end up with dozens of md files telling your agent to keep reading. That's the wrong place to stop.

Markdown documents aren't constraints. They're recommendations. Agents can read the CONTRIBUTING.md, AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, rules file, style guide, runbook, whatever, summarize them, quote from them, say "I've read the docs, and I'll do my best to follow them." They add more and more surface area that needs to be parsed and understood: "Use the existing logging conventions in the repository." Which? Where? "Use small functions." How small? "Run the tests before pushing." Which tests? Which command? Which environment? The agent has to process all of this, balance conflicting directives, and exercise judgment. It's in the judgment where the agents can stray.

In contrast, deterministic actions don't need judgment. "Read the docs and follow the coding style" becomes "Run the ./scripts/lint.sh, ./scripts/format.sh, ./scripts/test.sh scripts." The agent runs them and gets a pass/fail outcome. If one fails, the agent sees the exact error and has nothing to interpret or guess at. "I thought the rule meant…" becomes ./scripts/lint.sh. "Do the refactoring" becomes "Run the ast-grep or jscodeshift or sed tool to apply the transformation." The agent doesn't need to decide which files to update. The script does that, by design. You're boxing the agent into a sequence of deterministic actions.

This is a change in design paradigm from "teach the agent what you prefer" to "translate your preferences into deterministic actions." You can't run a markdown document. You can run a script, a checklist, a Makefile target, a GitHub Action. If you have a Makefile with make setup, make lint, make test, make build targets, the agent doesn't need to understand your coding philosophy. It just needs to run make lint and respond to the results.

The point isn't to dumb down the agent. The point is to make the environment unambiguous. An agent can still be smart when it executes a set of deterministic actions. It can read the failures, make corrections, and re-run the tests. It just can't step outside of the box. It can be clever within the constraints, but the box exists as a series of commands that either pass or fail.

This is why coding agents don't do this well. They want to be independent and explore the repo, read the files, build a mental model, and then make things happen. That works until it doesn't. The more md files you have, the more the agents think they have discretion. "The docs say to use snake_case, but this one existing file is camelCase. Maybe the docs are old." The agent is trying to be helpful, but it's not being deterministic.

Most AI models write replies that are hard to follow. So I added ASD-STE100, a plain-English standard written for aircraft maintenance manuals, to my coding agent's markdown rules. One rule says "Keep sentences to 20 words or fewer." As a script, that becomes MAX_SENTENCE = 20. When the agent ran the script over 10 of its own replies from one session, it found 9 failures. The script found them only after the replies were written, because nothing forced an earlier run. So the script goes in a hook.

I saw CI do this on a fix I sent to Forem. I don't write Ruby, and I had no Ruby installed, so CI was my test machine. My coding assistant wrote the fix and the tests. The first run failed, and the issue was in the test, not the code. That result did not depend on the assistant's opinion of its own work. But CI also passed an unused line, and only the reviewer caught it. A check only boxes in what it tests.

Full story: I Don't Write Ruby. A Fix I Sent Is Now in Forem.

If you want agents to do what you want, don't stop at md files. Write scripts.

Make every "please remember to" into a command. Every "we prefer" into a check. Every "before you push" into a pre-push hook. An agent can skip a local hook, so back it with a required CI job and a merge gate the agent has no rights to change. If a check fails, the agent can make corrections and run it again. That's how you box the agent into a deterministic sequence of actions. It's not a recommendation. It's a contract. And the agent can't ship work that fails the check.

articles.title: Plan Stamping, for Software
articles.description: Other professions worked out what a signature has to mean. We're about to need their answer.  A few...
articles.body_html:
Other professions worked out what a signature has to mean. We're about to need their answer.

A few months ago I had a coding agent build password reset for a small application. It took about five minutes. The email arrived, the link opened, the password changed, the user logged in with the new one.

I reviewed it. I approved it. Everything worked.

The reset link also worked a second time.

The implementation satisfied every behavior I thought to check while missing the invariant underneath them: once the reset succeeds, the token has to become useless. I wrote about that failure as a story about frameworks, because the lesson I took at the time was that mature abstractions carry knowledge forward. That's true. But there's a second thing in that story I walked past.

I was the human in the loop. My approval is on that code. And my approval established nothing.

That is the question I can't put down, and it is not really a question about software.

How do we establish trustworthy human responsibility for work that humans did not directly produce?

This article grew out of a conversation with Sylwia Laskowska following her article, We're Building AI to Replace Ourselves. What's the Plan? We were talking about junior developers, credentialing, and whether portfolios still demonstrate competence when agents can generate polished projects. Sylwia raised the possibility that software engineering might move toward something resembling architecture, with formal qualifications and supervised training. Neither of us was enthusiastic about excluding capable self-taught developers.

I've come around to part of her comparison, though not the part about credentials. What architecture and structural engineering have that we don't isn't a licensing exam. It's a definition of what a signature means.

Somebody already answered this

When a licensed engineer stamps a set of drawings, that stamp is not merely a gesture of approval. It represents a professional claim about the engineer's relationship to the work. Depending on the jurisdiction, that may require direct supervision and control, detailed knowledge of the design, or substantial independent verification and reworking. Simply reading through someone else's drawings and finding nothing obviously wrong is not necessarily sufficient.

Applying a professional seal without meeting the applicable requirements is commonly called plan stamping. Some jurisdictions treat it as grounds for disciplinary action, including fines, suspension, or loss of a professional license. The reasoning is straightforward: a seal is supposed to represent meaningful professional responsibility, not merely the presence of a qualified person's name on a document.

That is roughly a century of institutional thinking about the exact problem AI has just made urgent everywhere else. The professions that stamp things figured out early that a signature is worthless unless it certifies a specific relationship between the signer and the work, and then they went to the trouble of defining the relationship and punishing people who faked it.

Software has the signature. We have the approval on the pull request, the name in the audit log, the reviewer field in the ticket. What we generally lack is a shared definition of what that approval certifies.

The ceremonial approval

Imagine a team using agents to generate hundreds of changes a week, with a senior engineer assigned to approve them. The company can report that every change received human review. If that engineer lacks the time to examine the evidence, the authority to reject anything, or access to the assumptions behind it, the report is accurate and meaningless at the same time.

I don't have to imagine that one. I ran a one-person version of it and shipped a replayable reset token.

This is the failure mode worth naming now, because it arrives disguised as compliance. Nobody sets out to build a ceremonial approval process. It appears when production speeds up and review doesn't, and it is invisible from the outside because the artifacts of oversight are all present. There's a name in the log. The box is checked.

I've made a version of this argument before about code review as a security boundary: review is a good practice that cannot constrain what code is permitted to do, and treating it as a boundary means the boundary doesn't exist. The same shape applies here. An approval is a good practice that cannot by itself establish accountability, and treating it as accountability means accountability doesn't exist.

Responsibility without corresponding authority is not governance. It's liability assignment.

Four conditions

If a signature is going to mean something, the engineering boards suggest what has to be true. Theirs tends to reduce to direct control plus detailed knowledge, or doing the work over. Ours would need four things, and all four, because any one of them missing is enough to hollow out the other three.

An intelligible account. The reviewer needs to know what was proposed, what was checked, what remains uncertain, and what follows from acceptance. "The tests pass" is not that account. My reset flow passed its tests. The tests encoded the same assumption the implementation did.

Competence. The reviewer has to be able to recognize what's wrong, which means they need to have met this class of problem before. This is where the apprenticeship problem bites, and I'll come back to it.

Time. Not nominal availability. Enough time to actually examine the evidence for the volume of work arriving. Verification throughput is a real constraint, and it does not scale with the generation side.

Authority to refuse. The reviewer must be able to say no and have the no hold. A reviewer who can be overridden on schedule pressure is not a check on anything, and everyone in the organization learns that quickly.

Those four are the piece of this I'd want an organization to be able to answer for. Not "do you have human review," which every organization will say yes to, but "what did your reviewer have, and could they have stopped it."

Who gets to decide

There's a second consequence, and it may matter more for how people actually work.

The next professional divide may not run between people who use AI and people who don't. It may run between people authorized to make consequential decisions and people whose work is generated, evaluated, and approved by systems they don't control.

That divide can appear inside software teams, hospitals, design firms, and accounting practices. A small group defines requirements, approves exceptions, and accepts risk. Everyone else operates inside increasingly automated workflows. Some people gain extraordinary leverage. Others keep their jobs and lose the parts of them that involved judgment.

The useful questions are about distribution. Who can challenge the system's recommendation? Who can require more testing? Who can stop a release? Who answers afterward, and did they have the power to change the outcome beforehand?

There's a tempting answer here that I don't think survives contact with incentives: that the displaced production work reappears as verification work. Independent verification, requirements engineering, assurance, evidence management, and competency assessment are all real activities that may well grow. But if one engineer with agents does what five did, nothing guarantees four verification roles appear. A company can simply employ fewer people, underinvest in review, and find out later that its approval process was ceremonial. The need for assurance has never been the same thing as a willingness to pay for it.

The same caution applies to the shorter workweek. Productivity creates the possibility of more leisure. It does not decide who gets it. That's a choice organizations and societies make, not a feature shipped in a model update.

Where the next reviewers come from

Which brings me back to competence, and to Sylwia's original question about junior developers.

Judgment comes from experience. People learn by implementing imperfect solutions, investigating their own failures, absorbing criticism, and living with decisions they made a year earlier. I know a replayable token is a problem because I have spent time on the consequences of that category of mistake.

If agents do the introductory work and companies stop hiring beginners, we get a profession that demands experienced reviewers while closing the path that produces them. Every one of the four conditions above assumes a supply of people competent to review, and we are in the process of disrupting one of the principal mechanisms that has ever generated them.

Credentials don't fix this by themselves. A certificate establishes that someone passed an assessment, not that they'll exercise sound judgment in an unfamiliar situation. And the field has been built substantially by self-taught practitioners, so a licensure regime would exclude people who are currently among its best.

Sustained open-source participation is a better signal than a portfolio, for the reason that the artifact stopped being evidence a while ago. A pull request is another thing an agent can generate. The surrounding history is harder to fake: how someone finds a problem, argues about approaches, responds to review, chases a regression, and supports a change after it lands.

But there's an uncomfortable consequence to leaning on that. If open source becomes the informal proving ground for the profession, the cost of training and evaluating newcomers lands on maintainers who are already donating their time. We don't get to solve the apprenticeship problem by quietly outsourcing it to volunteers.

That one I don't have an answer to. It needs somebody to pay for mentorship who currently isn't.

What I'd ask instead

"Which jobs can AI replace?" sorts professions into safe and unsafe, as though the work inside each one were fixed. The more useful questions are narrower.

Which decisions are getting easier to generate and harder to justify? What evidence should accompany an AI-produced recommendation? Who is permitted to reject it? How does anyone acquire the judgment to do so? And what stops approval from becoming a name in a log attached to a process nobody can inspect?

The answers differ by field. A chatbot feature, a bridge, and a treatment recommendation carry different obligations. But all three turn on the same distinction, which is the one the engineering boards drew a century ago and wrote penalties for: producing an answer and being answerable for it are different acts, and only the second one requires that somebody actually understood the work.

We are issuing an enormous number of signatures right now without having decided what ours certify.

I'd rather we decide on purpose.

Thanks to Sylwia Laskowska for the conversation that prompted this article, particularly her questions about junior developers, credentials, and how people enter the profession as AI changes the work.

Sources on plan stamping: Hawaii DCCA, Notice Regarding Plan Stamping (HAR §16-115-10(4), §16-115-2; HRS §464-10); STRUCTURE magazine, Beware the Stamp.

articles.title: A Maintainer's Advice on Contributing to Open Source in 2026
articles.description: The ideal contributor   As an open-source maintainer, you imagine the ideal contributor as...
articles.body_html:
The ideal contributor

As an open-source maintainer, you imagine the ideal contributor as an individual that is excited about your project, uses it and understands it, and wants to contribute to make it better for themselves, others, or because of an exciting technical problem.
You get to share ideas with them, learn from each other, maybe even get to know them a bit as a person in the process, and they inspire you to do better work. A profoundly human, intellectual interaction, inspiring and fulfilling, sometimes even resulting in a life-long relationship.

When that happens, it is an amazing experience, absolutely my favorite part of building open-source software.

I still remember when Craig, whom we didn't know yet then, came out of nowhere and shared his proposal for formal language grammar for Wasp, a proper Latex document: I had to take a week to refresh my knowledge of type inference and language grammars just to be able to respond. The whole team looked together at that document, not believing the work put into it. He ended up doing 3 summer internships in a row with us, implementing a big part of Wasp compiler and language server, and was a delight to work with.

Or, another, more recent situation, when I got somewhat stuck on pushing Windows support for Wasp forward, and @nodtem66 came in with investigation and experiments of his own, effectively unblocking me and becoming a brainstorming partner for driving the feature forward. I remember being impressed by the thoroughness of the work from his side, there was that level of rigor to it that took me back to the uni times, and it was quite an inspiration at the moment.

The reality

However, for every such interaction, there is probably 10x or more low-quality contributions.

And I don't mean low-quality because the contributor is missing technical knowledge, but low-quality because motivation was never right: no real interest for the project, focus instead being on merging the PRs for the sake of merging them, to pump up the author's GitHub account or CV with the proof of contributing to popular open-source repos, or to win some kind of award (e.g. during Hacktoberfest).

What I find most demotivating regarding such low-quality interactions is that when I see a new PR, I can't help but get excited: maybe this is a "good" one, the one where rich, inspiring interaction will happen. But what most likely follows is a dissapointment, and this is a part of what grinds the open-source maintainers down with time.

How AI made it worse

The main thing that changed for worse recently though, with the rise of AI, is that it became very easy to create open-source contributions that look good at first, but there is no real substance or quality behind them.

Before, one could quickly assess the PR for quality: if it looked complex and good, the person behind it for sure had to put the effort and obtain a certain level of understanding of the codebase and the subject matter.
Effort was put in, so you didn't feel bad putting effort from your side also, while reviewing it.

Now, you often just can't know till you dive in deeper.

Good example is Craig's contribution of a Latex document with the new formal grammar for Wasp that I mentioned above. When Craig submitted that in 2021, I didn't think twice about investing a whole week of my own time to be able to review that PR properly. I was brimming with excitement. Even though I knew nothing about Craig.

Today, if I received such a contribution, my first assumption would be that it was AI generated, with no deep understanding of the matter by the author. I wouldn't dare invest a week, or even a day of my own time, to evaluate it.

And to be clear, it's not even about purely evaluating the correctness of the submitted work: maybe it is correct, maybe it works well, maybe it is even well designed. The problem is, I can't rely on the person behind it. I can't hope that there will be a rich, fulfilling cooperation coming out of this, resulting in new ideas, in growing together, creating something together. And if so, if the whole contribution is indeed primarily AI driven, then what is the point? If I wanted to tackle it myself like that, I will prompt my own AI, likely with a better prompt and better context.

This sucks. It sucks that my first assumption these days on seeing a contribution is that it is AI generated, and I wish it wasn't so, but that is how it is at the moment. It sucks for the maintainers, and it also sucks for the honest contributors that are putting in the real work.

What can one do then, as a new contributor to an open-source project, to surpass this?
I thought about this recently, and I believe it comes down to a single thing: building trust.

How to build trust as a new open-source contributor

Before, that was relatively easy: a well-crafted, quality PR would get you a long way.

Today, more is needed, and I will give some ideas below on how to do this, that would do it for me as an open-source maintainer.

Be sincere, be human

Be an honest human and treat others as such.

This is it really. It was always important, but now it is crucial. Everything else stems from it.

Don't treat the project and people behind it as resources or means to an end, e.g. just for getting a notch for your CV. Instead find a project for which you have an honest interest, and it will immediately show.

Also don't be shy to engage in conversation. Maintainers are also humans and will appreciate sincere interaction.

Coommunicate your motivation

Communicate why you are excited about the project, what you have used it for so far, why you want to contribute. You might think it is obvious, but it's often not. It helps maintainers "place you", figure out how to best direct you, what they can expect from you.

Don't use AI for writing (e.g. PR descriptions)

Don't let the AI write for you, or even enhance your writing. This goes for any text others will have to read really. Better to have it not be perfect, than to make others doubt if there is a human behind that text or not. Even if you are not native speaker and are just using AI to "fix" your text: either prompt it to only fix the most minor grammar issues, or use something else like Grammarly, to ensure it doesn't change your tone.

Own the contribution

Check the specific project's contributing guidelines, but most projects won't mind you using AI, as long as you own the contribution: you should own and stand behind every line of code and every decision in your PR, exactly as if no AI was involved. That means you've read it, run it, understood it, and you can explain and defend it under review.

Start with easier, smaller issues

Pick issues that are not demanding on maintainers to review, so they can get to know you and your work before having to invest a lot of time. Make it as easy as possible to review, and explain your reasoning and approach.

Agree with maintainers on what to work on before you start

Learn which issues would maintainers be happy with you taking on. Old issues might have become irrelevant, issues requiring a lot of "taste" for the project or issues touching core parts of the project might be quite mentally taxing to review, etc.

That said, just asking "what are good issues for a beginner" might not be enough. Some repos might have those organized and ready, but many don't, and it also depends on your skills and interests.

What is better is to come already with some suggestions of your own and ask if any of these would be right to start with. While also explaining why each of these is interesting to you and why you would like to tackle it. Even if none of those are a good starting issue, maintainers will now have a much better idea of what you are looking for and will be able to more easily suggest some other issue.

Use the project

Ideally, this would be the reason why you want to contribute: you are a user that wants to give back, make it better for themselves and others.

But even if this is not the case and you want to contribute for some other reason, e.g. because you really like the tech stack and want to gain some experience with it, you should take some time to use the project and learn about it, understand it better.

This will also help with coming up with the ideas for the issues you want to contribute to: you will identify parts of the project you think could be better, and can start from there.

Final thoughts

While it is harder to establish trust as an open-source contributor these days than it was before due to AI, there is a silver lining to it: solution is to be more human and more mindful, which was always the right way to do it.

articles.title: Trocar de provedor não deveria ser uma dor de cabeça
articles.description: Se você já trabalhou ou trabalha em startups, em um fluxo rápido de desenvolvimento de produto ou até...
articles.body_html:
Se você já trabalhou ou trabalha em startups, em um fluxo rápido de desenvolvimento de produto ou até mesmo criando o seu produto, deve saber que um produto pode e vai mudar em algum momento, devido à necessidade de novos investidores ou clientes, ou à decisão de algum stakeholder. Caso você não tenha experiência ou esteja começando agora nesse mundo de entregas rápidas, neste artigo eu pretendo te passar uma breve dica que provavelmente vai te economizar tempo de trabalho e reduzir as suas chances de ter dor de cabeça.

Sumário

  • Por que trocar de provedor
  • O provedor dentro do domínio
    • A modelagem acoplada
    • O código acoplado
  • E se o provedor mudar?
  • A solução
    • O domínio fala a própria língua
    • Um tradutor para cada provedor
    • Juntando tudo

Por que trocar de provedor

Acredito que o cenário mais comum e prático que eu possa dar para ilustrar o que eu quero te mostrar seja o caso em que você precise lidar com a mudança de um provedor de pagamento. Muitas coisas podem fazer com que uma empresa ou um produto cogite mudar o provedor, como: melhores taxas entre provedores, qualidade no suporte, maturidade do provedor e confiabilidade. Até mesmo o cenário em que o dono do provedor de pagamento é conhecido ou amigo da startup ou empresa em que você trabalha pode motivar essa mudança.

O provedor dentro do domínio

Imagine que chega a task para você fazer a implementação de um provedor de pagamento X dentro de um novo produto da empresa. Com prazo apertado e um único provedor, modelar tudo em cima dele parece o caminho mais rápido. Você faz a modelagem, faz a integração, tudo certinho: testado e funcionando. Mas aí, depois de alguns meses, chega a task para implementar um novo provedor de pagamento, e você percebe que vai ser uma dor de cabeça, porque tanto a modelagem quanto o código do domínio foram feitos com o vocabulário do antigo provedor, tornando tudo acoplado. Essa é uma situação que não é nada interessante de se resolver, mas é bem previsível de se combater.

A modelagem acoplada

O código acoplado

Aqui foi exemplificado o impacto na modelagem, mas, além dele, o código também teria outros problemas, como a repetição de código e inúmeras verificações.

final class ReleaseProduct
{
    public function __invoke(Order $order): void
    {
        $isPaid = match ($order->provider) {
            'stripe' => $order->stripe_status === 'succeeded',
            'mercadopago' => $order->mercadopago_status === 'approved',
        };

        if (! $isPaid) {
            return;
        }

        $order->product->release();
    }
}

final class RefundOrder
{
    public function __invoke(Order $order): void
    {
        match ($order->provider) {
            'stripe' => $this->stripe->refund($order->stripe_payment_intent_id),
            'mercadopago' => $this->mercadoPago->refund($order->mercadopago_payment_id),
        };
    }
}

E se o provedor mudar?

Eu tive o prazer de ter uma ótima liderança técnica e experiente que, antes mesmo de me deixar colocar a mão na modelagem, me mostrou as seguintes questões: "E se o provedor mudar, o que fazer? Qual a consequência de mudar do provedor X para o Y?" Sinceramente, no começo eu não fazia ideia do que fazer. Foi aí que me foi apresentada a ideia de fazer uma modelagem e um código agnóstico de provedor (provider-agnostic).

Na computação, um dispositivo ou programa de software é considerado agnóstico ou agnóstico de dados se o método ou formato de transmissão de dados for irrelevante para a função do dispositivo ou programa. Isso significa que o dispositivo ou programa pode receber dados em múltiplos formatos ou de múltiplas fontes e ainda assim processá-los de forma eficaz. — Wikipédia, tradução livre

Uma maneira prática de absorver essa ideia, e que me ajudou bastante, foi pensar: caso determinada informação possa ter um caminho diferente, tanto a modelagem quanto o código devem se comportar da mesma maneira, independentemente do caminho. No nosso exemplo, a informação é "o pagamento foi concluído", e os caminhos são o Stripe e o Mercado Pago.

Pagamento é só o exemplo que escolhi, mas a mesma ideia aparece em vários outros lugares: provedor de autenticação (Auth0, Cognito, Firebase Auth), envio de e-mail (SES, SendGrid, Mailgun), armazenamento de arquivos (S3, Google Cloud Storage) e envio de SMS (Twilio, Zenvia). Se você usa Laravel, já usa isso no dia a dia: o Mail e o Storage funcionam do mesmo jeito, seja qual for o driver configurado por trás.

A solução

O domínio fala a própria língua

Para tornar o código e a modelagem agnósticos de provedor, você vai precisar entender o que é domínio. Talvez você já tenha ouvido falar sobre DDD; é dele que vem esse termo. Não vou entrar no tema por completo (recomendo que você leia sobre o assunto depois), mas vou explicar brevemente o que seria esse tal domínio.

Entenda o domínio como a área de conhecimento e as regras do problema que o seu produto resolve. No código, ele vira a parte central, que reúne essas regras e entende como resolver o problema. No exemplo que estou utilizando, a nossa área de conhecimento e as regras são de pedido, então o nosso domínio tem tudo o que é necessário para resolver isso.

Agora que sabemos disso, você já deve ter notado que cada provedor tem uma nomenclatura para as informações de que ele precisa ou que retorna. Um pagamento concluído, por exemplo, é succeeded no Stripe e approved no Mercado Pago. Já o nosso domínio usa os próprios nomes, paid ou canceled, escolhidos por você ou pelo seu time, e os nomes dos provedores nunca chegam até ele.

Olhando para a modelagem: a tabela orders guarda só o vocabulário do domínio. O provedor vira apenas um dado (provider), e o id dele fica em uma coluna genérica (provider_reference).

Schema::create('orders', function (Blueprint $table) {
    $table->id();
    $table->integer('amount_cents');
    $table->string('status');
    $table->string('provider');
    $table->string('provider_reference')->nullable();
    $table->timestamps();
});

enum PaymentStatus: string
{
    case Pending = 'pending';
    case Paid = 'paid';
    case Canceled = 'canceled';
}

enum PaymentProvider: string
{
    case Stripe = 'stripe';
    case MercadoPago = 'mercadopago';
}

final class Order extends Model
{
    protected function casts(): array
    {
        return [
            'status' => PaymentStatus::class,
            'provider' => PaymentProvider::class,
        ];
    }
}

Um tradutor para cada provedor

O próximo passo é lidar com essa diferença de nomenclatura entre os provedores. Para isso, vamos criar uma classe que faz a tradução da nomenclatura da API para o que temos no nosso domínio. Esse tradutor é um adaptador (adapter), e todos os adaptadores seguem o mesmo contrato, a porta (port) que o domínio define. Essa camada de tradução, como um todo, é o que o DDD chama de camada anticorrupção (Anti-Corruption Layer).

                   DOMÍNIO  (fala "paid", "canceled")
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  ReleaseProduct      RefundOrder      HandleWebhook │
  └──────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────┘
                             │ depende só do contrato
                 ┌───────────▼────────────┐
                 │ PaymentGatewayContract │  ← porta
                 └───────────┬────────────┘
             ┌───────────────┴────────────────┐
  ┌──────────▼───────────┐       ┌────────────▼───────────┐
  │ StripeGateway        │       │ MercadoPagoGateway     │  ← adaptadores
  │ "succeeded" → paid   │       │ "approved"  → paid     │    (traduzem)
  └──────────┬───────────┘       └────────────┬───────────┘
             ▼                                ▼
         API Stripe                   API Mercado Pago

Depois vem a porta, o contrato que todo provedor precisa seguir:

interface PaymentGatewayContract
{
    public function charge(Order $order): string;

    public function status(string $reference): PaymentStatus;

    public function refund(string $reference): void;
}

E um adaptador para cada provedor. É aqui, e só aqui, que o vocabulário de cada um aparece:

final class StripeGateway implements PaymentGatewayContract
{
    public function __construct(private StripeApi $api) {}

    public function charge(Order $order): string
    {
        return $this->api->createPaymentIntent($order->amount_cents)->id;
    }

    public function status(string $reference): PaymentStatus
    {
        return match ($this->api->getPaymentIntent($reference)->status) {
            'succeeded' => PaymentStatus::Paid,
            'canceled' => PaymentStatus::Canceled,
            default => PaymentStatus::Pending,
        };
    }

    public function refund(string $reference): void
    {
        $this->api->refundPaymentIntent($reference);
    }
}

final class MercadoPagoGateway implements PaymentGatewayContract
{
    public function __construct(private MercadoPagoApi $api) {}

    public function charge(Order $order): string
    {
        return $this->api->createPixPayment($order->amount_cents)->id;
    }

    public function status(string $reference): PaymentStatus
    {
        return match ($this->api->getPayment($reference)->status) {
            'approved' => PaymentStatus::Paid,
            'cancelled', 'rejected' => PaymentStatus::Canceled,
            default => PaymentStatus::Pending,
        };
    }

    public function refund(string $reference): void
    {
        $this->api->refundPayment($reference);
    }
}

Juntando tudo

A configuração diz qual provedor está ativo:

// config/payments.php
return [
    'default' => env('PAYMENT_PROVIDER', 'stripe'),
];

Um resolver sabe qual adaptador corresponde a cada provedor:

final class PaymentGatewayResolver
{
    public function for(PaymentProvider $provider): PaymentGatewayContract
    {
        return match ($provider) {
            PaymentProvider::Stripe => app(StripeGateway::class),
            PaymentProvider::MercadoPago => app(MercadoPagoGateway::class),
        };
    }
}

E o container do Laravel junta os dois: entrega o adaptador do provedor ativo para qualquer classe que peça o contrato.

final class AppServiceProvider extends ServiceProvider
{
    public function register(): void
    {
        $this->app->bind(
            PaymentGatewayContract::class,
            fn () => app(PaymentGatewayResolver::class)
                ->for(PaymentProvider::from(config('payments.default'))),
        );
    }
}

Com isso, aquelas classes do começo do artigo deixam de saber qual provedor está por trás:

final class ReleaseProduct
{
    public function __invoke(Order $order): void
    {
        if ($order->status !== PaymentStatus::Paid) {
            return;
        }

        $order->product->release();
    }
}

final class RefundOrder
{
    public function __construct(private PaymentGatewayContract $gateway) {}

    public function __invoke(Order $order): void
    {
        $this->gateway->refund($order->provider_reference);
    }
}

Se amanhã chegar a task de um terceiro provedor, o trabalho é criar um adaptador novo, adicionar um caso no enum PaymentProvider e uma linha no PaymentGatewayResolver. A tabela orders, o ReleaseProduct e o RefundOrder continuam iguais.

articles.title: My AI Agent Said 'Done.' It Wasn't. A Field Guide to Trusting Nothing an Agent Tells You
articles.description: Last week, my coding agent reported a clean deploy. Green checkmark, tidy summary, even a polite "Let...
articles.body_html:
Last week, my coding agent reported a clean deploy. Green checkmark, tidy summary, even a polite "Let me know if you'd like me to verify anything further." It had not run the tests. The migration it "applied" had never touched the database.

Nothing crashed. Nothing alerted. That's the part that should scare you.

The feed is trying to tell us something

Spend ten minutes on the DEV front page right now and a pattern jumps out. Not "AI is amazing." Not "AI is over." Something more specific:

  • A developer discovers Codex had been quietly hammering their SSD for months — nobody noticed.
  • Someone reruns their local AI's work from scratch: it invented 162 Python packages, and 161 of them "came back" as plausible-looking fiction.
  • An agent gives the right answer, then confidently writes down that it was wrong.
  • A whole genre of posts about agents that got prompt-injected because they trust everything they read.
  • Spec drafts for the things agents are missing: undo, human approval for destructive tools, real authentication.

Read between the lines and the community isn't asking "can agents code?" anymore. We've collectively answered that. The new question is: why do they report success when nothing succeeded?

Agents fail like broken CI, not like broken code

When your code breaks, it usually fails loudly: an exception, a red test, a crash. When an agent fails, it frequently fails silently, because the agent's job is to produce a narrative, and a narrative can be true or false independently of the world.

Call it the Green Checkmark Problem: the agent optimizes for a plausible completion report, and "everything worked" is the most plausible completion report there is.

The failure modes cluster into three buckets:

1. Confident hallucination

Invented packages, invented APIs, invented file paths. The scariest part isn't that it happens — it's that the output looks like the output of a successful run. Plausible names, plausible logs, plausible numbers.

2. Silent no-ops

The command "ran." The file was "written." The migration was "applied." Except it never was — wrong working directory, swallowed error, a timeout interpreted as success. In workflow tools, two branches can write to the same row and both report success. Nobody notices for months, until somebody's SSD fills up.

3. Self-deception

The agent evaluates its own work, gets confused, and records the wrong verdict — sometimes even correcting a right answer into a wrong one. When the verifier and the doer share a brain, confirmation bias isn't a bug; it's the default.

A field guide: trust nothing, verify everything

Here's the checklist I now run on every agent action that claims to have changed the world:

1. Never accept a claim of success. Accept only evidence.
"Tests pass" is a claim. Exit code 0 captured from your shell, not the agent's, is evidence. "Deployed" is a claim. The new version string served in production is evidence.

2. Re-observe the world, not the log.
After any mutation, go look at the actual thing: query the database, hit the endpoint, open the file. Ten seconds of direct observation beats ten minutes of agent-generated summary.

3. Give every destructive action an undo.
The community spec drafts for "undo for agents" exist for a reason. If your agent can delete, drop, or overwrite, wrap it in something reversible before you need it, not after.

4. Put a human gate on the irreversible.
Approving destructive tool calls feels like friction right up until the day it feels like a save point. One confirmation click is cheap insurance.

5. Make the agent prove negatives.
Ask it: "What would you have seen if this had failed?" If it can't answer, it wasn't checking. An agent that can't describe the failure path has almost certainly never looked for it.

6. Log the delta, not the dialogue.
Agent transcripts are great stories and terrible audit logs. Diff the actual artifacts — files, schemas, deployed builds — and store that as your source of truth.

The uncomfortable takeaway

The paradox of 2026 is that agents got good enough to do real work, which means their failures are now real failures — just wearing a green checkmark. The tools are catching up: undo specs, approval middleware, adversarial "second-opinion" reviewers. But the culture shift is ours to make.

Treat your agent like a brilliant new hire who is a terrible self-reporter. Give them real work. Verify the receipts. Never let them grade their own homework.

The green checkmark is not a fact. It's a claim. Check it anyway.

articles.title: Vibecoding met 34-year-old railway software
articles.description: TL;DR. After Urda, a four-hour Renfe map went viral beside 34-year-old signalling. We have reached an...
articles.body_html:
TL;DR. After Urda, a four-hour Renfe map went viral beside 34-year-old signalling. We have reached an inflection point where a finished-looking demo can be believed as a real product, even next to safety-critical infrastructure.

Contents

  • What "legacy" means on a high-speed line
  • What Vía Libre actually did
  • The inflection point vibecoding just hit
  • What the criticism actually said
  • Human error or system error, through a legacy lens
  • What juniors should take away
  • Sources

On 28 October 2026, a Renfe AVE collided with a stationary Iryo train near Urda, in Toledo, Spain. Sixty-nine people lost their lives. My thoughts are with their families and with everyone affected. The investigation is still open, and nothing written here treats any cause as settled.

Two days later, a different story went viral. Álvaro Hernández published Vía Libre, a web map of Renfe trains built in about four hours from public GPS data. Colours marked delays. Screenshots travelled faster than the nuance.

Those two stories sit on the same week for a reason juniors keep hitting at work: legacy systems look slow and ugly until you learn why they are hard to change, and AI has made it so easy to ship something that looks finished that people can believe a demo can stand in for a real product.

This piece uses Urda and Vía Libre to hold both ideas at once, with Vía Libre as the heaviest example of that belief so far.

What "legacy" means on a high-speed line

The Madrid-Seville AVE corridor still runs under LZB (Linienzugbeeinflussung), a German continuous train-control system installed for the line's opening in 1992. That is 34-year-old railway software still sitting in the safety path.

In plain words, the track and the train keep talking so the system can supervise speed and brake automatically if needed. When LZB drops, traffic can fall back to BSL (bloqueo de señalización lateral: the side signals that organise blocks of track) with ASFA as onboard protection that reacts when the train passes beacons. That stack is old, layered, and certified for lives, not for demos.

Press coverage after Urda repeated the same timeline: LZB arrived because Europe's later standard, ERTMS, was not ready in 1992; Adif has been migrating Madrid-Seville to ERTMS Level 2; the physical work finished, but putting the new system into service still needs tests and authorisation from the rail safety agency.

A railway signalling engineer told La Tribuna de Ciudad Real that LZB gear is robust and near the end of a useful life of about three decades. The former head of the State Agency for Railway Safety had already called LZB obsolete in the Senate weeks before the crash. Replacement is underway. It is not a git merge.

On top of that world sits a thinner layer: Renfe's open data, including near-real-time vehicle positions in GTFS-RT, updated every 15 seconds for AVE and long distance (20 for Cercanías), under a CC BY 4.0 licence. That feed is for passengers and builders. It is not the signalling stack. Confusing the two is how vibecoding stories start.

Layer What it is What it is not
Signalling (LZB / ERTMS / ASFA) Safety path that supervises speed, routes, and braking A passenger map
Open data (GTFS-RT) Public positions for builders and riders A control desk or safety case

What Vía Libre actually did

Álvaro said he wondered how long a Renfe monitor would take, noticed that each train's GPS position was public, and had something working in three to four hours. Vía Libre plots Renfe services on a map of Spain with a delay semaphore and Adif incident notices on one screen.


Screenshot of Vía Libre. Source: El Español / Omicrono, 30/10/2026.


Mobile view of Vía Libre shared on X, 30/10/2026. Post: x.com status 2116271528396677542.

That is a real win for open data and for fast prototyping. Anyone can see how far a public feed plus a clear UI can go in a morning.

It is also where the new risk starts: a browser reading GTFS-RT does not supervise braking curves, does not interlock routes, and does not carry a safety case, yet it can look finished enough that people treat it as more.


Screenshot of Álvaro Hernández's original thread, reshared on X, 31/10/2026. Post: x.com status 2116679379468120546.

The inflection point vibecoding just hit

Vibecoding means asking an AI for code and shipping what comes back while it "feels" right, without owning the failure modes. Readers already know a four-hour map cannot retire LZB or finish ERTMS. That part is settled.

What is new is the inflection. AI has made it cheap enough to ship something that looks finished that a builder, or an audience watching screenshots travel, can honestly believe a demo-grade build can stand in for a real product. Not as a joke: as something that could run in a real business, or sit next to a system people already trust.

Most vibecoding stories stop at a SaaS landing page or an internal tool. Vía Libre is the heaviest case yet, because the thing it seemed to rival, in the public conversation after Urda, was safety-critical railway infrastructure.

That belief is the new risk. A map that paints delays in green, yellow, and red looks like monitoring. Screenshots travel like a product launch. The speed of the build can read as proof that the old stack was optional. None of that turns an open-data viewer into a control system, but the look of finish is strong enough that people can confuse the layers without trying.

Why legacy stays slow

Legacy railway systems stay slow to change for boring, expensive reasons:

  • Safety certification. Every real change has to be re-tested and signed off before passengers ride on it. Think of a release process where "ship" means an outside auditor stamps the build, not a green CI job.
  • Interlocking. Trackside logic that stops two trains from claiming the same block of track at once. Like a lock or mutex on a shared resource, except the resource is a stretch of rail and the failure mode is a collision.
  • Layers added after earlier incidents. Extra checks and fallbacks piled on over decades. Like patches nobody wants to delete, because nobody is sure which one still holds a crash path shut.
  • Ageing kit and scarce spares. Gear from the early 1990s eventually leaves the vendor catalogue. Replacing a board is not npm update; it can mean hunting a part that is no longer made.
  • Testing on a live corridor. A lot of the real proving has to happen on the actual line, often at night when passenger trains are not running. You cannot spin up a full high-speed clone in staging.
  • AESF authorisation. Spain's State Agency for Railway Safety (AESF) has to authorise bringing a new or changed structural subsystem, including signalling, into service. Until that file is approved, the new stack does not carry passengers, no matter how ready it looks on paper.

That cost does not disappear because a morning build looks polished.

Álvaro drew the line himself. As quoted by El Español and La Razón, he did not want Spanish trains controlled by a "Paco-APP" built in a morning. His point was about political will to use what already exists for safety, not about swapping signalling for a weekend build.

Fair enough. The case still matters as evidence of the inflection: if even a careful builder's demo can travel as if it answered a railway, then the bar for "looks ready" has moved.

A four-hour map like this can still prove the feed is readable, shame bad UX, and start a useful argument about transparency. Keep those. What changed is the gap: "looks finished" and "is a product" used to be obviously far apart. Vibecoding shrank that gap enough that the belief is now part of what you have to manage.

What the criticism actually said

The pushback around Vía Libre clustered into a few themes. No need to pile onto individuals.

I do not question Álvaro's good faith in trying to help or put another solution on the table. Most of the criticism came from the sense that he had underestimated the infrastructure. My own take is milder: I think he simply had not informed himself well enough before framing it that way.

  • Already existed. People said the map was not new: Renfe already had an official real-time viewer, and other private trackers existed. Putting open data on a map is not inventing the railway.
  • Front end, not signalling. Others said it was mostly a nicer front end on a feed Renfe already publishes: useful to look at, not a monitoring or signalling product. A passenger map is not a control desk.
  • Read the numbers. A third theme was about reading the numbers. Public feeds can lag or fail. Some trains are estimated from the timetable. Press pieces noted that "real time" on the site animates between updates, that operators such as Iryo and Ouigo are missing from that feed, and that the famous 93-of-119 delay count was one snapshot on a drivers' strike day, not an official punctuality score for the whole network.

There was praise too. People shared the site as a clear way to see delays, and some welcomed an independent view while still saying it should not replace the operators.


Official Renfe viewer (tiempo-real.largorecorrido.renfe.com). Source: Railway Gazette, 12/03/2026, Renfe screenshot.

Human error or system error, through a legacy lens

After Urda, public debate often split into "human error" versus "system error." Through a legacy lens, that split is too thin.

What official sources and the press have established so far:

  • Around 08:30 the LZB failed on that stretch.
  • The control centre authorised the AVE to run under "marcha normal" instead of "marcha a la vista", which caps speed at 40 km/h when you are running with degraded protection.
  • The preliminary report from AITAT, the body that investigates accidents, talks about a "chain of failures, instructions and actions" without the needed safety barriers kicking in.
  • The technical and judicial investigations are still open. Every hypothesis still is.

There is a human decision in that chain. That it is the cause is not proven. Investigators also look at maintenance, protocols, and why backup layers did not stop the train.

That is how you read a decades-old stack: a person acts inside procedures, fallbacks, and machines that age. Naming one person without the chain is the same mistake as celebrating one map without the stack.

In software we call the careful version a blameless postmortem: after an incident, ask which layer was missing, not only who typed the command. People fail. Good systems assume that and put nets underneath.

Legacy railways already try to do that with continuous supervision, side-signal fallback, and automatic braking. When those nets tear, the lesson is to repair and replace the nets with the same seriousness that certified them, not to pretend a dashboard could have held them.

What juniors should take away

If you are early in your career, this week is easy to misread. Either "one app exposed the state" or "one person's mistake caused the crash." Neither is enough.

  • Treat open data as a gift with limits. Credit the licence. Show how old each value is. Decide what the UI does when the feed dies.
  • Respect legacy before you rewrite it. Ask what certification, interlocking, or incident history made it look "ugly."
  • Use AI to learn and prototype. Notice when a finished-looking demo starts to feel like a product, to you or to your audience.
  • When something breaks, look for the chain: inputs, fallbacks, monitoring, human procedures, and the layer that should have caught the mistake.
  • Say out loud what your weekend build does not do. That sentence is part of the product, especially when the screenshots travel faster than the caveat.

Vía Libre shows how fast a readable view can appear when the data is public, and how easy it is now for that view to travel as if it answered more than it does. Urda shows why the systems underneath move on a different clock.

The useful junior skill is not dismissing legacy, and not treating vibecoding as a shortcut past it. It is learning to read both, and to name the gap between a finished-looking demo and a product that can carry real trust.
